newsitem.title: USA: U.S. House sub-committee to vote on D.C. package.
newsitem.headline: U.S. House sub-committee to vote on D.C. package.

text.p: A key U.S. House panel Thursday morning is expected to vote on a broad District of Columbia initiative bill similar to one proposed by President Clinton earlier this year.

The House Government Reform and Oversight Committee's D.C. sub-committee will vote on a bill circulated by chairman, Rep. Thomas Davis of Virginia, that would hand over responsibility for the city's multi-billion dollar unfunded pension liability to the federal government.

The bill would increase the federal share of Medicaid reimbursement from the current 50 percent to 70 percent. It would also authorize a small U.S. annual payment to the District of $140 million in the 1998 fiscal year.
Currently the city receives an annual payment of $660 million from the federal government. President Clinton in his D.C. package called for elimination of the annual payment.
Davis' bill would continue the federal payment after 1998 at "unspecified amounts". The bill would also require the District to have a balanced budget in FY 1998.
The bill authorizes D.C. to borrow a total of $500 million from the Treasury Dept. over 15 years to finance its accumulated operating deficit and for short-term capital needs.

D.C.'s delegate to Congress, Eleanor Holmes-Norton, (D) told a Washington T.V. station that the provision is a "important sleeper in this bill. That's about a half a billion dollars. As long as that debt was there, the District was going to have a Control Board for the foreseeable future," she said.
The bill would reform D.C. revenue bond authority "to modernize and treat the District as the states are treated," the outline of Davis' proposal said.
The bill creates a 10-year Economic Development Corporation to "promote job creation and employment of D.C. residents through assisting business development and retention."
The Corporation would be initially funded with $50 million and would get half of D.C.'s allotment of revenue bond authority.

The bill calls for about $325 million over five years in federal tax relief for the city with $75 million in tax credits to be allocated by the Corporation. That provision is similar to one authorized by the House Ways and Means Committee last week.
The federal government would assume the costs of D.C. courts, estimated at about $136 million in FY 1998. The U.S. Bureau of Prisons would take over responsibility for housing D.C. felons.
